title: Growing comfrey Bocking 14
subtitle: The permanent fertility plant that earns its spot in every kitchen garden.
excerpt: Comfrey Bocking 14 is a sterile hybrid grown for its leaves, which decompose quickly into a potassium-rich mulch or liquid feed. Plant root crowns in spring and the plant returns year after year with almost no care.
sourceNotes: Bocking 14 cultivar information and fertility figures from Lawrence Hills, Comfrey: Past, Present and Future (1976). UK growing guidance cross-referenced with Henry Doubleday Research Association records and current Garden Organic material. Soil biology notes from general organic farming literature.

glossaryTerms.definition: A sterile hybrid of Russian comfrey (Symphytum x uplandicum) selected at the Bocking trial ground by Lawrence Hills of the Henry Doubleday Research Association. It does not set viable seed, so it stays where you put it.
The portion of root with a bud or growing point at the top, cut from an established comfrey plant and used for propagation. Each crown grows into a full plant within one season.

content.text: Comfrey is a deep-rooted perennial grown for its leaves rather than as a food plant. The leaves are high in potassium, nitrogen, and phosphorus. Cut and lay them as a mulch, steep them in water for a liquid feed, or drop them into the bottom of a planting hole. The plant dies back in winter and returns from its crown each spring without replanting.
. Non-sterile comfrey sets seed prolifically and becomes a weed in a single season. Bocking 14 produces no viable seed. Plant it once and it stays where you put it.

Comfrey tolerates partial shade and does well at the edge of a compost heap, along a fence line, or under trees where little else will grow productively. It prefers a moisture-retentive soil but manages in most conditions once established. Avoid planting it in a bed you intend to cultivate: the roots are brittle and any fragment left in the ground grows a new plant.

(also called root cuttings or thongs) rather than seed. Seed sold as comfrey is usually non-sterile species. Root crowns of Bocking 14 are available from specialist UK suppliers in late winter and early spring. Three to five plants is enough for a medium kitchen garden; each plant yields four or five cuts per season.

Plant root crowns from March to April, or in October when soil is still warm. Dig a hole about 8 cm deep. Place the crown bud-side up (the growing tip is usually slightly off-white or pink against the darker root). Cover with 5 cm of soil. Space plants 60 to 90 cm apart.

Keep the area weed-free for the first season. Comfrey is slow to establish and can be swamped by grass and nettles in its first year. From the second year, it competes well and needs very little attention.

In the first year, take one or two cuts only to let the plant establish. From the second year, cut the stems down to 5 cm above the ground up to five times between May and September. Cut before the plant flowers for the highest nutrient content; flowering redirects energy to seed formation (though Bocking 14 sets no viable seed, the nutrient balance still shifts).

The cut leaves wilt rapidly. Use them fresh as a mulch around hungry crops (courgettes, tomatoes, potatoes work well). Stack them in a barrel of water to make liquid feed, or lay them in the bottom of a potato or bean trench before planting.

Cut the stems to the ground in October or November when the leaves die back. Leave the cut material on the soil surface as a mulch or add it to the compost heap. The crown overwinters in the ground and regrows in March or April without any intervention.

attrs.heading: When it goes wrong
attrs.intro: Established comfrey rarely fails; most problems occur in the first season.

items.symptom: Crown planted but nothing appeared after 6 weeks
items.cause: Planted too deep, cold soil, or crown planted upside down.
items.fix: Gently dig around the crown. If it is rotting, the position was too wet. If it looks dormant (firm and pale), be patient: comfrey is slow to break dormancy in a cold spring. Replant at 5-6 cm depth if you suspect it was too deep.

items.symptom: Plant grew well but the leaves are very small
items.cause: Crowns establish slowly; soil may be very poor or dry.
items.fix: Top-dress with a handful of general-purpose compost in spring. Water during dry spells in the first season. By year two the plant should reach full size.

items.symptom: Comfrey appearing in beds where it was not planted
items.cause: Root fragments distributed during soil movement.
items.fix: Remove shoots as soon as they appear, before they establish a root system. Do not rotovate an established comfrey plant: the root fragments spread the plant across the garden.

attrs.title: Propagating from cuttings
attrs.body: To increase your comfrey stock, lift an established plant in autumn and chop the roots into 5 to 8 cm sections. Each section with a dormant bud grows a new plant. Store the cuttings in just-moist compost over winter and pot them into 9 cm pots in February. Plant out in April. One mature plant can produce 20 to 30 root cuttings.
